title: RefereeBench: Are Video MLLMs Ready to be Multi-Sport Referees?
article_content: This paper presents RefereeBench, a benchmark for evaluating multimodal large language models as automatic sports referees across 11 sports. The dataset includes 925 curated videos and 6,475 expert-authored question-answer pairs covering foul detection, foul and penalty classification, reasoning, entity perception, and temporal grounding. All data were manually curated by certified referees. The study finds that even leading proprietary MLLMs remain well short of dependable officiating performance, with top systems reaching only around 60% overall accuracy and the best open-source model around 47%. The authors also show that adding audio can improve performance by roughly 16 percentage points, highlighting the role of multimodal evidence in officiating.

market_context_source.title: The rise and limits of AI officiating in sports
market_context_source.article_content: Reuters’ coverage of AI officiating across sports provides broader context for why RefereeBench matters. The article surveys how leagues and technology vendors are expanding use of semi-automated offside, ball-tracking, line-calling, and decision-support systems, while still facing resistance over transparency, trust, edge cases, and the role of human judgment. It frames officiating technology as a competitive and governance battleground involving leagues, broadcasters, athletes, and fans rather than a purely technical challenge. That makes RefereeBench especially relevant: the paper supplies evidence that current multimodal models are still not reliable enough to replace human referees across sports. The source is valuable market context because it connects benchmark results to the real deployment pressures and credibility thresholds shaping adoption.
